image/numbers: A program cannot see a picture: all it can work with is numbers. So first, an image has to become numbers.
image/rgb: Take this tiny color image, four pixels by four. Each pixel, one small square of color, is three numbers: how much red, green and blue.
image/flat: Lay them all out in one row: pixel after pixel, red, green, then blue. Four times four times three: forty eight numbers.
image/vector: A list of numbers in a fixed order is called a vector: here, the whole image as one object. The order tells the numbers apart: the first is always the top left pixel's red.
image/big: A thirty two by thirty two color photo works the same way: three thousand and seventy two numbers in one vector.
arrow/point: Now a vector of just two numbers, three and two. On a graph, they say where to go: three across, then two up.
arrow/arrow: Or draw it as an arrow: from the origin, the corner where both numbers are zero, out to the point.
arrow/name: In 1846, the Irish mathematician William Rowan Hamilton called such a line, with a length and a direction, a vector: Latin for carrier. It carries you from the origin to the point.
arrow/dim: Each number moves you along a direction of its own: the first across, the second up. Two directions make a flat plane, with two dimensions: a vector's dimension is how many numbers it holds.
arrow/three: A third number adds a third direction, out of the page: three dimensions, like a room.
arrow/more: Past three, no picture fits, but the count still works: the image's forty eight numbers make a forty eight dimensional vector.
list/list: Longer vectors are written as lists. This x holds four numbers: three, minus one, four and two.
list/len: Four numbers, so x is four-dimensional. Python calls that count its length, and NumPy writes its shape as four, comma: one row of four.
list/reals: In math, the real numbers, all the points on the number line, are written as a double-struck R. Lists of four of them make R four.
list/in: So x in R four says x is a list of four real numbers. The sign in the middle means “is in”.
list/index: Each entry has an index, its position, in square brackets. Python counts from zero, so x of zero is the first entry: three.
list/last: So the last of four is x of three, which is two, and there is no x of four: the last index is one less than the count.
ops/two: Take two vectors, u and v: u is one, two, and v is three, minus one.
ops/add: Add them entry by entry, first with first and second with second: u plus v is four, one.
ops/tail: On the graph, that is one arrow after the other: follow the arrow u, then v from where it ends, and the walk ends at four, one.
ops/scale: Multiply by a number, and every entry is multiplied: two times u is two, and four. The arrow keeps its direction and grows twice as long, which is why this is called scaling.
ops/neg: A negative number turns it around: minus one times u is minus one, and minus two.
ops/same: Adding needs the same number of entries. Give v a third, and u has none to match it: NumPy refuses.
